en: *The Verses for Paying Homage upon Rebirth*, one fascicle,
compiled by the Śramaṇa Shandao.
It exhorts all sentient beings to aspire to be born in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, the realm of Amitābha Buddha.
In the state,

This is done solely with the desire to maintain continuity of practice, focus the mind, and assist in accomplishing the benefit of rebirth.

so that its benefits may reach far into distant ages. Why is this?

exhorting you to recite them, pay homage, and maintain mindfulness so that you may certainly be born in that land.

He asked: "Now, if one wishes to encourage others to attain rebirth [in the Pure Land]..."
I do not yet know how to settle the mind, initiate practice,
and perform deeds so that one will certainly attain rebirth in that land.
He replied:
If one truly desires to be born in that land,
as stated in the *Contemplation Sūtra*,
one will certainly attain rebirth by possessing the three minds.
What are the three?
First is the sincere mind,
which refers to performing the bodily act of prostrating before that Buddha.
With the vocal karma, they praise and extol that Buddha;
with the mental karma, they single-mindedly contemplate and observe that Buddha.
Whenever these three karmas are initiated, [they do so directed toward him].
It must be true; therefore, it is called the mind of utmost sincerity.
Second is the profound mind.
This is precisely true faith:
to believe and know that one's own self is an ordinary person possessed of afflictions,
with meager roots of goodness.
Cycling through the three realms and unable to escape the burning house,
I now truly believe in the fundamental great vows of Amitābha.
Furthermore, by reciting the name—
even as few as ten times or a single time—
one will certainly attain rebirth there.
Even for a single thought-moment, there is no doubt;
therefore, it is called the profound mind (*adhyāśaya-citta*).
Third is the mind of dedication and aspiration (*pariṇāmanā-praṇidhāna-citta*).
All roots of goodness performed are entirely dedicated toward the aspiration for rebirth;
therefore, this is called the mind of dedication and aspiration.
One who possesses these three minds will certainly attain rebirth.
If even a single thought of the mind is lacking, one will not be able to be born [there].
This should be understood as it is fully explained in the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*.
Furthermore, as stated in Vasubandhu’s *Treatise on the Pure Land*:
"If there are those who wish to be reborn in that land,
they should be encouraged to practice the five gates of mindfulness."
If one possesses these five gates, one will certainly attain birth [in the Pure Land]. What are the five?
The first is the gate of bodily action: prostration.
That is to say: with single-minded devotion and profound reverence, join the palms,
offer incense and flowers as an offering,
and prostrate before Amitābha Buddha.
As for ritual practice, one should exclusively worship that Buddha,
taking the end of one's life as the limit,
without intermingling it with other rituals.
Therefore, this is called the gate of prostration.
Second is the gate of verbal praise,
which consists of single-mindedly praising the physical marks and the radiance of that Buddha’s body.
Because it encompasses the radiant physical marks of all the noble assembly,
as well as the radiance of all the jewel adornments within that land,
it is therefore called the "Gate of Praise."
Third is the gateway of mental action through recollection and observation.
This refers to single-mindedly recollecting and contemplating that Buddha,
as well as the physical forms and radiance of all the noble assemblies.
The adornments of the land and so forth are as described in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
This applies at all times, except during sleep.
Because one constantly recollects, constantly remembers, constantly contemplates, and constantly observes these matters and so forth,
it is called the "Gate of Observation.
Fourth is the "Gate of Making Vows."
What is called single-mindedness:
whether by day or by night,
at all times and in all places.
Regarding the merit produced through the three types of action and the four modes of deportment,
regardless of whether it was performed at the beginning, middle, or end,
one must in all cases sincerely make a vow from the depths of one's heart to be reborn in that land.
Therefore, it is called the gate of making vows.
Fifth is the gate of dedication,
which refers to single-minded devotion.

One should deeply give rise to sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) for the roots of goodness one has created oneself, as well as for all the roots of goodness performed by those of the three vehicles and five destinies—

When these five gates are fully possessed, one will certainly attain rebirth.

It should be known that one should further be exhorted to practice the four methods of cultivation,
employing them to spur on the three minds and the practice of the five recollections.
One will swiftly attain rebirth there. What are these four?
First is reverent cultivation.
This refers to reverently prostrating before that Buddha and all those holy assemblies;
therefore, it is called "cultivation through reverence.
One should take the end of one's life as the limit for this practice.
Vowing not to desist is cultivation over a long period.
Second is cultivation without remainder.
This means exclusively reciting the name of that Buddha;
exclusively mindfulness of, visualization of, prostration to, and praise of that Buddha and all the assembly of holy ones,
without intermingling with other activities.
Therefore, it is called "cultivation without remainder.
One takes the end of one's life as the limit,
vowing never to desist.
This refers to long-term cultivation.
Third is uninterrupted cultivation,
which means continuous, reverent prostration.
Recite their names and offer praise;
maintain mindfulness and contemplation;
dedicate the merit and make vows.
Because the mind continues in succession without being interrupted by other karmic activities,
it is called "uninterrupted cultivation" (*nirantara-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, it is not interrupted by the afflictions of greed or hatred.
One should repent immediately upon committing an offense,
not allowing it to be separated by a thought, a period of time, or a day,
so as to remain constantly pure.
It is also called uninterrupted cultivation;
taking the end of one's life as the limit,
one vows not to cease.

and they act in accordance with conditions as they arise.

but instead send them directly to exclusively recite the name?
What is the underlying intention?
The answer is:
It is because sentient beings have heavy afflictive obstructions;
while the objects are subtle, their minds are coarse.
Consciousness flutters and the spirit soars;
thus, contemplation is difficult to accomplish.
For this reason, the Great Sage felt compassion and pity.

why is it that the manifested realm appears as many?

The answer is:
All Buddhas are equally realized;

The answer is:
the *Amitābha Sūtra* and the *Contemplation Sūtra* state:
The light of that Buddha is immeasurable;
it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without any obstruction.
Because he exclusively contemplates and brings to mind all sentient beings,
gathering them in and never abandoning them, he is named Amitābha.
The lifespan of that Buddha and that of his people lasts for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas;
therefore, he is named Amitābha.

Even with as few as a single utterance or a single thought,
one will certainly attain rebirth;
this matter is thus certified and verified.
Therefore, it is called the *Hunian jing* (Sutra on Protective Mindfulness).
Next, the text below states:
"If one invokes the Buddha for rebirth..."
It is constantly protected and remembered by as many Buddhas of the six directions as there are grains of sand in the Ganges;
therefore, it is called the *Hunian jing* (Sutra of Protection and Remembrance).
Now that this superior vow has been made, [it shall be fulfilled].
It is to be relied upon.
O sons of the Buddha, why do you not exert yourselves to depart?
— *The Verses of Worship and Praise for Rebirth* (Wǎngshēng lǐzàn jì)
